s: Part three.
Spawning subagents and passing context.
This is task statement one point three: configure subagent invocation, context passing, and spawning.
By the end of this part, you'll know what a subagent can and cannot see, how to write a delegation it can act on, and how findings should come back.
Let's start with a picture.
Write a handover note for the colleague covering your shift, and you learn quickly what travels and what doesn't.
You spent the morning on a problem.
They didn't.
Everything you worked out reaches them only if it's on the note.
"Finish the thing we discussed" is not a note.
It's a reference to a conversation they weren't in.
A worker agent is that colleague.
With one difference that makes the discipline stricter.
It can't phone you.
There's no shared memory behind the note.
No history it can look up.
And nobody on the other end to answer a question.
Whatever you left out is gone.
But that strictness has an upside, and it's the whole reason to delegate.
A colleague who starts with a clean desk isn't carrying your morning's clutter.
The technical version.
A subagent's context window starts fresh.
The Agent SDK documentation says it plainly.
The only content you pass from parent to subagent is the Agent tool's prompt string.
So any file paths, error messages or decisions the subagent needs must go directly into that prompt.
So what exactly crosses the boundary?
The subagent receives four things.
One.
Its own system prompt.
That comes from the prompt field of its AgentDefinition, or the markdown body of a subagent file.
Two.
The delegation message, meaning the Agent tool's prompt string.
Three.
The project CLAUDE.md files, loaded through setting sources.
Four.
Its tool definitions, inherited, or narrowed by its tools list.
And what does it not receive?
It does not receive the parent's conversation history, or any tool result in it.
It does not receive the parent's system prompt.
It does not receive preloaded skill content, unless the skill is named in its skills field.
And it does not receive the parent's output style, or auto memory.
Question one.
Here's the scenario.
A platform team puts its code review standards in the coordinator's system prompt.
The coordinator follows them.
The three reviewer subagents it spawns ignore them.
The standards apply to every subagent, on every run.
The team doesn't want compliance to depend on the coordinator remembering to restate them.
Project setting sources are enabled.
Where should the standards go?
Take a second.
A new contractor isn't handed the manager's personal notebook.
But every contractor gets the site safety handbook on day one.
If a rule has to reach every contractor, it goes in the handbook.
The answer.
Put the standards in the project CLAUDE.md, which subagents load.
Or in each reviewer's own definition prompt.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: move the standards to the top of the coordinator's system prompt, and repeat them at the end.
Why?
The parent's system prompt never crosses the boundary.
So no amount of emphasis there reaches a subagent.
Wrong: put them in the coordinator's conversation history, which subagents supposedly read through the parent tool-use link.
Why?
They don't.
The parent_tool_use_id field correlates messages for tracing.
It does not share context.
Wrong: have the coordinator paste the standards into every delegation prompt.
Why?
That works only when the coordinator remembers.
That's the exact dependency the team wants removed.
And it costs tokens on every call.
Hold on to this line.
If every subagent must know it every time, put it where subagents load it on their own.
In CLAUDE.md, or their own definition.
Next, the delegation prompt itself.
Question two.
Here's the scenario.
In a Claude Code session, the main agent spends twenty minutes running a slow integration suite.
It isolates one failing test, its assertion error, and the cause: a timezone default in a date helper.
It then delegates with the prompt "Fix the failing test we found; use the fix we agreed on."
The subagent reruns the full suite.
It changes the test's expected value, instead of the helper.
And it takes eighteen turns.
What went wrong?
Take a second.
A doctor hands over mid-shift with a sticky note saying "finish what we discussed."
The colleague wasn't in the room.
So they repeat every test, and may treat the wrong thing.
A proper handover names the patient, the finding, and the decision already made.
The answer.
In exam terms, "we" and "the fix we agreed on" refer to nothing the subagent can see.
Rerunning the suite and editing the test are direct consequences of missing inputs.
The fix is to rewrite the delegation as a self-contained work order.
What goes in it?
One.
The file path.
Two.
The test name.
Three.
The command to reproduce it.
Four.
The exact error text.
Five.
The locked decision.
Here, that's to change the helper to use UTC, and not touch the test.
Six.
What's out of scope.
And seven.
The shape of what to return.
For example, just the diff and the passing test output.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: raise the subagent's maxTurns, and use a larger model.
Why?
More turns and a bigger model can't recover information the subagent was never given.
Wrong: add the timezone decision to the project CLAUDE.md.
Why?
CLAUDE.md does reach subagents.
But a one-off fix decision is the wrong lifetime for a durable project file.
And it still leaves out the test and the error.
Wrong: give the subagent the Agent tool, so it can delegate the slow suite run.
Why?
That pushes the same missing context one layer further down.
And it adds cost.
The notes have a near twin.
A coordinator delegates "Audit checkout's dependencies using the approach we agreed on."
But the parent had already read the manifest.
It had found an ancient pinned version.
And it had agreed with the user that no major version bumps are allowed this cycle.
The subagent searches broadly.
It proposes a major bump.
And it takes nineteen turns.
Same fix.
A self-contained work order, with the manifest path, the finding, the locked no-major-bumps decision, and the return shape.
Here's the heuristic to remember.
Hold on to this line.
If you can't write the delegation prompt without saying "as discussed", the work is not separable yet.
It belongs in the parent conversation.
And notice the distinctive symptoms of a missing handoff.
There are three.
One.
A subagent that says it can't find a file the parent just read.
Two.
One that asks a question nobody is there to answer.
Three.
One that re-derives an analysis the parent already paid for.
Each looks like model incompetence.
Each is a missing handoff.
And the fix is explicit injection of context.
Not more turns.
Not a bigger model.
So, a delegation prompt is an interface.
It carries inputs, locked decisions, scope, and the return shape.
Or the child is guessing.
Now, how the coordinator chooses which subagent to use.
Question three.
Here's the scenario.
A support coordinator has three subagents: billing-disputes, shipping-status, and account-security.
Each has a detailed prompt, and the right tools.
But all three descriptions read "Helps customers resolve their issues."
About a third of shipping questions go to billing-disputes.
What's the fix?
Take a second.
A hospital switchboard lists three departments as "helps patients."
Callers keep landing in the wrong ward.
Relabel them broken bones, heart problems, and children under twelve, and the operator routes correctly.
Without a longer manual.
The answer.
A subagent's description field is the selection signal Claude matches tasks against, at the moment it picks a worker.
It's a routing rule, not documentation.
Three identical descriptions leave the coordinator guessing.
So you rewrite each description as a routing rule.
It says when to use it, what it handles, and what it does not handle.
For example. shipping-status answers where-is-my-order and delivery date questions.
And it does not handle refunds, charges or logins.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: add routing rules to the coordinator's system prompt, like "send tracking questions to shipping-status."
Why?
That patches a description defect with a prompt rule.
It holds until the rule loses the competition for attention.
And every new subagent needs another patch.
Wrong: give all three subagents every tool, so a misrouted question can still be answered.
Why?
That breaks least privilege.
And it hides the misrouting.
Wrong: move the coordinator to a larger model.
Why?
It still has nothing to tell three identical descriptions apart.
This theme returns in the chapter on tool design and integration.
There, the same rule applies to tool descriptions.
Fix the defect where it lives, not with a prompt patch.
Hold on to this line.
The description is how the coordinator picks.
So write it as a rule for when to pick it.
Next, the tools list, and its look-alikes.
This is where the exam sets name collisions against each other.
So slow down.
In plain words.
If a worker must never do something, don't hand it the means to do it.
A note saying "please don't" is not the same as withholding the key.
If a trainee must never open the safe, you don't give them the key along with a polite note.
You simply don't give them the key.
The manager keeps theirs.
The technical version.
A subagent's tools field is an availability list.
A tool left out is not in that agent's session at all.
So the action can't be taken, whatever the model decides.
There's also disallowedTools.
It removes named tools, and it's applied first.
That's structural enforcement.
The first rung of the enforcement ladder we meet in part four.
Now the three look-alikes.
One at a time.
One.
Skill frontmatter allowed-tools, with a hyphen.
It pre-approves listed tools for the invoking turn.
And it restricts nothing.
Two.
The SDK option allowedTools, one word, in camel case.
It's a permission list.
It decides which calls run without prompting.
Three.
A subagent's tools list.
That one restricts.
So: permission, restriction, pre-approval.
And a fourth name to keep separate. readOnlyHint, a tool annotation.
It's a scheduling hint, about whether a tool can run in parallel with other read-only tools.
It is never authorization.
The Model Context Protocol specification even requires clients to treat annotations as untrusted, unless they come from a trusted server.
So a tool marked readOnlyHint true can still write to disk.
Question four.
Here's the scenario.
A policy-lookup subagent is meant only to read refund policy and order records.
It inherits every tool.
And last week, it issued a refund on its own.
The security lead wants it to be impossible for this subagent to call refunds_issue.
While the main agent keeps that tool.
What do you do?
Take a second.
The answer.
Set the subagent's tools list to only the read tools it needs.
So refunds_issue is not in its session.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: list refunds_issue under allowed-tools in a skill's frontmatter, with a note marking it forbidden.
Why?
Skill allowed-tools pre-approves, and restricts nothing.
Wrong: mark the lookup tools with readOnlyHint.
Why?
Annotations are hints, not authorization.
And hinting the read tools does nothing to remove the refund tool.
Wrong: add a prompt line saying never issue refunds.
Why?
It's probabilistic.
And the subagent's instructions have already failed once.
A note on the study material here, because the sources use different names.
The lesson two slide deck uses the older names.
It calls the delegation tool the Task tool.
And it uses allowed_tools, with an underscore, when describing which tools an agent may use.
The written notes use the current names.
The Agent tool, which was renamed from Task in Claude Code version two point one point sixty-three.
And tools, for a subagent's own availability list.
Recognise both spellings.
The notes add a practical wrinkle.
Current releases emit Agent in tool_use blocks.
But they still show Task in the system init tools list, and in the permission denials list on the result.
So detection code should match both names.
On the exam, if a question says Task, read it as Agent.
And if a question frames allowed tools as a restriction on what a subagent can do, answer in the question's terms.
While remembering that in the current SDK, the restricting field is tools, and allowedTools is the permission list.
Hold on to this line. tools restricts. allowedTools permits.
Skill allowed-tools pre-approves.
And readOnlyHint authorises nothing.
A few more mechanics complete the picture.
An AgentDefinition requires two fields: description and prompt.
It also accepts optional fields.
These include tools, disallowedTools, model, skills, memory, mcpServers, initialPrompt, maxTurns, background, effort, and permissionMode.
If model is left out, the subagent uses the main model.
Subagents can also be defined as files in the .claude/agents/ folder.
They're markdown, with a small header that requires only name and description.
If a programmatic definition and a file share a name, the programmatic one wins.
And every message produced inside a subagent carries a parent_tool_use_id.
So you can trace which delegation it belongs to.
Now, how findings come back.
Question five.
Here's the scenario.
A regulatory research system has search subagents.
Each one summarises ten sources into a paragraph of prose, before handing it to a synthesis subagent.
The briefings read well.
But auditors must be able to trace every claim to its source and retrieval date.
And almost none can be traced.
What's the fix?
Take a second.
A researcher photocopies ten articles, writes a one-page summary, and throws the copies away.
When an editor asks where a figure came from, nobody can say.
A labelled index card per fact, with its source and date, is what makes the summary checkable.
The answer.
In exam terms, summarising into prose silently drops attribution.
Once ten sources become one paragraph, no downstream agent can recover which claim came from where.
So you return findings as structured objects that keep content separate from metadata.
Such as the source URL, the retrieval time, and a confidence value.
With claim identifiers linked to source identifiers.
And the synthesis stage's output schema must keep that claim-to-source mapping intact.
Or the chain of provenance breaks right there.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: instruct the synthesis subagent to cite carefully and include dates.
Why?
It can't cite what the prose handoff already threw away.
Wrong: pass the full text of every source to the synthesiser.
Why?
That floods its window.
And it still doesn't enforce claim-to-source links.
Wrong: have the search subagents write longer summaries.
Why?
Longer prose is still prose.
The chapter on context management and reliability picks up provenance in more depth.
Hold on to this line.
Hand findings back as labelled records, not paragraphs.
And make the next stage keep the labels.
And what happens when two findings disagree?
Question six.
Here's the scenario.
Two researcher subagents report different list prices for the same competitor product.
One comes from a vendor datasheet dated March.
One from a reseller page retrieved last week.
The synthesis subagent keeps the newer figure, and drops the other without comment.
The client has said pricing conflicts must be visible to a human reviewer.
What should the output be?
Take a second.
Two witnesses give different times for an accident.
A good clerk writes down both statements, and flags the difference for the judge.
Instead of quietly keeping whichever witness sounded more certain.
The judge decides, not the clerk.
The answer.
In exam terms, a subagent must never silently pick one of two conflicting claims.
The correct output records a conflict object, holding both claims with their sources.
It marks it unresolved.
And it escalates it to the coordinator, which surfaces it to the reviewer.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: keep the higher-confidence figure, and note the rating.
Why?
That's still a silent resolution.
And stated confidence is not evidence.
Wrong: average the two figures, and flag the result as an estimate.
Why?
That manufactures a number neither source reported.
Wrong: re-run both researchers until they agree.
Why?
That burns budget.
And it can converge on the wrong figure, because the sources genuinely differ.
Hold on to this line.
When sources conflict, record both, mark it unresolved, and let a human decide.
One last mechanic before we leave this part.
Parallelism at the tool level follows its own rule.
Within a single turn, read-only tools, such as Read, Glob and Grep, can run at the same time.
Tools that change state, such as Edit, Write and Bash, run one after another, to avoid conflicts.
Custom tools default to sequential.
They opt in to parallel scheduling with readOnlyHint.
And again, that hint affects scheduling only.
Never safety.
That's part three.
If you remember one thing, make it this.
The child knows only what you write down.
Write the work order.
Write descriptions as routing rules.
Withhold tools rather than forbid them.
And hand findings back as structured records that keep their sources, and their conflicts, visible.
Coming up in part four: enforcement and handoffs in multi-step workflows.
